questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an archive's contents reflect
questions.stem: Planning a new civic hall, an architect must ask which drawings the archive actually kept.

options.text: Which records the collecting office chose to retain, and why
Which drawings best represent the building as it actually looked

options.text: Which drawings were made by the most distinguished hand
options.misconception: judges survival by the reputation of the maker

options.text: Which drawings were made before the building was altered
options.misconception: assumes keepers selected by date of the subject

questions.explanation: Archives hold what later offices chose to keep, and selection is made for reasons of prestige, usefulness and space. The drawings an architect finds are a filtered record.
questions.hint: Ask what the collecting office wanted.

questions.stem: Briefing a school conversion, an architect must plan a check of a claim that the chapel's roof was raised in 1712.

questions.topic: The limits of a customs book
questions.learningObjective: State what a customs book establishes
questions.stem: An architect asking what a customs book can establish finds it lists 88 loads of timber and 31 of stone for 1743.

options.text: That the building site consumed 88 loads of timber in 1743
options.misconception: reads a port entry as a site delivery

options.text: That timber and stone were equally valuable, since both are listed
options.misconception: infers value from the fact of listing

options.text: That the customs house recorded those entries for the port that year
That the site was built in 1743, since the materials were imported then
options.misconception: dates a building from a shipment

questions.explanation: A customs book records transactions as the port office saw them, so it fixes what was entered, not what a building used or when it rose. The entries belong to the office.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a subscription list really evidences
questions.stem: For a public subscription list, an architect must explain why it shows more about publicity than about money.

answer.exemplar: A subscription list is made to persuade, to record credit and to reassure donors that their names will be seen, so it is evidence of how a project was sold rather than of what was paid. The amount set against each name is what the subscriber was asked for, not what was received, and the order of the names is arranged to flatter. Where a later receipt book survives, the two can be compared and the difference described. The brief should therefore use the list to show the character of the campaign and its backers, and should look elsewhere for what the town actually paid.

questions.explanation: A subscription list records what people were asked for and how they wished to be seen, not what the town received. It is strong evidence of publicity and weak evidence of money.
questions.hint: Ask what the list was for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Oral tradition and layers of collection
questions.learningObjective: Judge what an oral tradition can establish

stimulus.body: Account given in 1903 by a stonemason's apprentice, said to have been told to him by the oldest man in the parish: that the market cross had stood where the lime avenue now runs until the year of the great frost, when it was taken down for the new paving. The apprentice added that no one living could remember the cross itself.

questions.stem: An architect must weigh an oral tradition about a market cross against the fabric of the square.

options.text: That the whole story is invented, since no written record of it survives
options.misconception: requires a written record before accepting testimony

options.text: That the market cross stood on the lime avenue until the great frost
options.misconception: takes a collected story as an eyewitness account

options.text: That the frost of which the story speaks must have been in the seventeenth century
options.misconception: dates an undated reference from a later story

options.text: That the story was collected in 1903 and carries the layers of its telling

questions.explanation: An oral tradition is a collection of layers, each telling shaped the last. It is good evidence of how the square was remembered in 1903, and weak evidence of any century's layout.
questions.hint: Date the telling, and every telling before it.

questions.explanation: An unfamiliar legal term is an invitation to check, not to assume. The architect should find how the word was used in comparable leases of the period, note any local gloss.

options.misconception: assumes copying always improves accuracy

options.text: That the earlier date must be right, since the event cannot have been misremembered
options.misconception: assumes the first record is never wrong

That the demolition happened twice, once in 1801 and once in 1811
options.misconception: turns a documentary conflict into two events

questions.explanation: A conflict between two archives is a fact about the archives, and each date attaches to the job its document was doing. One may record the order to demolish and the other the completion.

questions.learningObjective: Read what a letter's silence indicates
questions.stem: In a 1765 letter about a roof leak, a friend writes only that the matter is settled and nothing more.

options.misconception: reads a formula as a technical report

questions.explanation: A private letter says what its writer assumed and what its reader knew, so a phrase that seals a subject means the details were elsewhere. Reading the silence as reassurance over-reads the writer.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a chronicle from a minute book
questions.stem: An architect compares a 1465 chronicle entry on a guildhall fire with a 1467 minute book on rebuilding.

options.text: The chronicle narrates the event, the minute book records the decisions taken
The minute book is the better source because it is more detailed

options.misconception: merges a narrative with a record of decisions

questions.explanation: A chronicle and a minute book answer different questions: one narrates what happened to a readership, the other records proposals.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a victors' archive needs care
questions.stem: For the victors' archive, an architect must explain why it should be treated with caution.

answer.exemplar: The victors wrote the account that survived, and their paperwork is full of the language of justification, while the losing side's records were seized, hidden or destroyed. What comes down therefore shows the winner's account of the contest more fully than the loser's version of it. An architect can still use such a file, and often must, since it may hold the only measurements of a demolished building, but the brief should say plainly whose voice the archive carries, look for any surviving trace of the other side, and treat the silences as the work of victors rather than as evidence that nothing happened.

questions.explanation: An archive from the defeated side is usually written, kept and shaped by the victors, so it carries their account more fully than the other. It remains usable.
questions.hint: Ask whose voice the archive carries.

options.misconception: assumes a collector gathered everything worth keeping

options.text: That the old market cross was the only building the surveyor cared about
options.misconception: infers interest from what one collector kept

options.text: That the collection is dominated by one building, which shaped it
That the blank sheet proves the collection was incomplete when it was made
options.misconception: infers incompleteness from a blank sheet

questions.explanation: A collector's choice of what to bind shapes the archive that follows. Thirty-three of 41 sheets showing one building tells the architect about the collector's interest, not the town's buildings.
questions.hint: Ask what the collector was interested in.

questions.explanation: A check is worth making only if evidence could fail it. Comparing the stone's character against the quarry's records can support or undermine the claim.

questions.topic: Oral tradition and layers of collection
questions.learningObjective: Date the layers of a collected tradition
questions.stem: A 1903 account of a cross at Coldwick describes its removal in the year of the great frost.

options.text: The architect should date the removal to the great frost of 1746
options.misconception: names a date the account does not give

options.text: The architect should treat the year of the great frost as 1809
options.misconception: picks a frost year without evidence

options.text: The architect should seek the collecting date and the layers beneath the telling
The architect should treat the removal as proven, since a tradition records it

questions.explanation: A dated phrase in an undated account gives a layer of recollection, not a date. The architect must find when it was collected and work back through the tellings to a document naming the year.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a legal term should be researched
questions.stem: For a lease research section, an architect must explain how an unfamiliar legal term should be researched.

answer.exemplar: The work of an unfamiliar term is to narrow the range of meanings the document could bear, and every stage of that narrowing should be written down. The architect should first see whether the lease itself glosses the word, then search deeds of the same estate, other leases of the same period and any later legal opinions on comparable wording. The surrounding facts matter as much as the dictionary sense, since a term describing a share of a wharf points to a division of the wharf and not to a share of its income, unless the context shows otherwise. Where the range of meaning cannot be closed, the brief should say which readings remain open and what would settle them, rather than choosing one silently.

questions.explanation: Researching an unfamiliar term means narrowing the range of meanings the document could bear, using the lease's context and comparable deeds of the period. Where the meaning cannot be fixed.
questions.hint: Narrow the range, then say what is left.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two charters need not contradict each other

stimulus.body: Copy of a charter of 1402 granting the borough the right to hold a weekly market on the green. Copy of a charter of 1426 reciting the earlier grant and adding that the market be held on the second day. Both are enrolled copies made by the same hand in the fifteenth century.

questions.stem: An architect finds two charters that appear to disagree about the market day.

options.text: That the later charter may recite the earlier and add terms of its own
That the 1402 charter must be genuine and the 1426 one a later forgery
options.misconception: condemns a later copy without any internal test

options.text: That the market must have moved to the second day in the year of the second grant
options.misconception: reads a recital as a change in practice

options.text: That the charter hand proves both documents were written at the same time
options.misconception: infers date from a single scribal hand

questions.explanation: A later charter that recites an earlier one and adds terms is a normal legal form, not a contradiction. The architect should read the two as a sequence in which the terms were restated and extended.
questions.hint: A recital adds, it does not always change.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Planning a check of a claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a claim should be checked
questions.stem: For the checking section, an architect must explain how a claim about a building should be checked.

answer.exemplar: A check begins by stating the claim in a form that can be answered yes or no, and then by asking what evidence could answer it the other way. If the claim is that the roof was raised in 1712, the evidence might be the joinery, the sequence of the roof timbers, a dated payment, or a drawing of the roof before and after, and each of these could fail to support the claim. The brief should record the test chosen, the reason it was chosen, and what the result was, including a negative result. A claim checked in this way can be reported with its confidence attached, whereas a claim merely repeated by later writers can only be reported with somebody's opinion attached.

questions.explanation: A check begins by stating the claim so it can be answered, and by identifying evidence that could answer it the other way. A claim tested in this way can be reported with its confidence attached.
questions.hint: State the claim, then look for a refutation.

That timber supply in the port was steady across the eighteenth century
options.misconception: extends one carried-forward entry into a trend

questions.explanation: An entry marked as continuing from an earlier book is not a fresh count for the year in which it stands. The architect can use it for the earlier figure and for the clerk's habit.
questions.hint: Check whether the entry was newly counted.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a conflict caused by repair rather than rebuilding
questions.stem: An architect finds that one register records a wall built in 1590 and another, written 30 years later, records the same wall as new.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a letter's silences can be used for
questions.stem: For the private letter section, an architect must explain what a private letter's silences can be used for.

answer.exemplar: A private letter is written to one reader for one purpose, so its silences are selective in a way that a formal return's never are. Where a correspondent mentions a crack in a wall and passes over the roof, that may mean the roof was not his business, that the reader knew all about it, or that the letter was in a hurry. What the silence can still do is narrow the range of what the writer thought worth troubling the reader with, and that is sometimes useful for dating repairs or for locating a dispute. The brief should describe the silence in those terms, and should resist the temptation to treat the letter's reticence as a technical assurance.

questions.explanation: A private letter's silences are shaped by its purpose and its reader, so they narrow what the writer thought worth mentioning rather than proving anything about the building.
questions.hint: Silences narrow, they do not prove.

That the bridge at the ford was rebuilt of stone in 1523

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a public notice really proves
questions.stem: For a public notice section, an architect must explain why a notice proves less about a building than it seems to.

answer.exemplar: A public notice is written to achieve an immediate effect: to summon a jury, to warn of a scaffold, to announce a rate or to advertise a sale. Its words are therefore selected for the response they will produce, and silence in it carries little weight, since the writer had no reason to mention anything beyond the immediate business. What the notice does establish firmly is its own date, its occasion and the fact that the matter was considered important enough to announce. That can be decisive for dating a repair contract or a closing of a street, and the brief should use it for that, while looking to the accounts, minutes or fabric for anything about the state of the building.

questions.explanation: A public notice is written for an immediate effect, so its words are chosen for the response they produce and its silences mean little. It is good evidence for its date and occasion.
questions.hint: A notice proves its occasion, not the fabric.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a victors' file must be read with care
questions.stem: For the victors' archive section, an architect must explain why the file needs to be read with care.

answer.exemplar: The victors of a contest write the account that survives, because they control the offices, the record office and the fire that may or may not have taken the other side's papers. Their surviving file is therefore thorough on their own claims and thin, in a patterned way, on the claims of those they defeated. That pattern is itself a historical fact about the settlement and can be described with some precision: which petitions are absent, which suits are missing, which families appear only as defendants. The brief should read the archive for what it establishes about the victors' own procedure and intentions, and should treat the gaps as evidence of power rather than as evidence that nothing was ever claimed.

questions.explanation: The victors' file is thorough on their own claims and thin, in a patterned way, on those of the defeated. The gaps are evidence of power, and the brief should read them as such.
questions.hint: The gaps are evidence of power.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how to trace a legal term to its use
questions.stem: For a term research section, an architect must explain how an unfamiliar term in a lease should be traced.

answer.exemplar: The tracing of a legal term should leave a trail the client can inspect. The architect begins with the document itself, noting the immediate context, the parties and the subject of the grant, and asks what the parties would have meant by it in that setting. Then the term is searched in comparable instruments of the same estate, in the accounts of the same office and in any later dispute that quoted it. Each stage either narrows the sense or reveals that the term was used loosely. Where the sense cannot be closed, the brief should present the two strongest readings, say which facts each would fit, and recommend a search that would settle the point rather than presenting one reading as though it were certain.

questions.explanation: Tracing a legal term should leave a trail the client can inspect: the document's context, comparable instruments of the same estate, and any later dispute that quoted it. Where the sense stays open.
questions.hint: Leave a trail the client can follow.

answer.exemplar: A check that is not written down has not been done, because the reasoning behind a result is what later readers need and what the architect himself will forget within a year. The record should state the claim in a testable form, name the evidence consulted, note the date of each item so that later finds can be judged against the moment of the check, and record the result including a null one. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a writer's silence should be used
questions.stem: For a second correspondence section, an architect must explain how a writer's silence should be used.

answer.exemplar: Silence in a private letter is a fact about the letter, and it is worth using precisely because it is controlled by the writer's purpose. A letter about a payment will not mention the state of the roof, and a letter about the roof will not mention the rent. The architect should therefore ask what the letter was doing, and read the omissions as a map of the writer's concerns rather than as a record of the building. Where a silence is conspicuous, as where a writer praises a building without naming its defects, that is a rhetorical silence and may carry the opposite sense, which is why the surrounding language has to be read before anything is concluded.

questions.explanation: Silence in a letter maps the writer's concerns rather than the building's condition, and conspicuous silences can be rhetorical. The architect should read omissions against what the letter was doing.
questions.hint: Read omissions against the writer's purpose.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read a chronicle entry as a told account, not a record of building

stimulus.body: From the chronicle of the abbey of St Werburgh, kept in the sixteenth century: anno 1523, a great frost, and the bridge at the ford at Coldbeck was carried away with the water, and the townsmen of Coldbeck sued the abbey for the loss of their way to the market, and the matter was long in the law before it was ended. A later hand has written in the margin that the dispute lasted three years.

questions.stem: A chronicle entry about a bridge carried away by frost is weighed by an architect against the minute books.

options.text: That the bridge at Coldbeck was rebuilt in stone in 1523
options.misconception: reads an event as a completed repair

options.text: That the townsmen of Coldbeck had a right of way across the abbey ford
options.misconception: reads a disputed claim as an established right

options.text: That the chronicle records how the event was told, including a dispute
That the abbey was obliged by law to rebuild the bridge at once
options.misconception: infers an obligation from a chronicle entry

questions.explanation: A chronicle entry belongs to a narrative written for a readership and carries what the writer thought fit to tell, including a quarrel. It is good evidence of how the loss was described.
questions.hint: It tells how the event was told.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Plan how to present a victors' archive in the brief
questions.stem: An architect must plan how to present the victors' archive in the brief.

options.text: By presenting it as the town's record, since the town has kept it for three centuries
options.misconception: assumes custody implies impartiality

options.text: By omitting it, since a biased archive is worse than none
options.misconception: prefers an empty record to a qualified one

options.text: By citing only the documents that mention the rising of 1653
options.misconception: restricts the evidence to the loudest part

options.text: By naming whose account it is, and marking where it goes silent

questions.explanation: A victors' archive is a rich source with a known direction, and the brief gains from using it than hiding it. Naming whose account it is and marking its silences lets the reader weigh it as evidence.
questions.hint: Name the account, then mark its silences.
